text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London closed slightly lower after responding belatedly to an initially weak performance in New York. Moreover, improved crop prospects in Europe weighed on prices. October lost 60 cents to close at $322.30, while December gave up $1.20 to close at $319.70 per tonne.

Raw sugar futures in New York closed a thinly-traded session lower pressured by commission house selling. There was no fresh news to influence prices. October lost 2 points to close at 11.51 cents/lb, while March gave up 4 points to close at 11.77 cents/lb. The outer months lost between 1 and 2 points.

UNITED STATES - The United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) raised its forecast of the 1997/98 US sugar crop to 7.67 million short tons, raw value, up slightly from its previous forecast and 5.7 per cent above estimated production for 1996/97. In its monthly world supply-and-demand report, USDA pegged 1997/98 beet sugar production at 4.3 million tons, unchanged from last month and up 6 per cent from 1996/97. The department forecast 1997/98 cane sugar production at 3.36 million tons, up 2.7 per cent from its July forecast and 5.1 per cent higher than in 1996/97. In the coming weeks, USDA must decide on the import quota for 1997/98 (October/September). USDA set the quota at 2.31 million short tons in 1996/97, based on a 'stocks-to-use' ratio target of 15.5 per cent. US sugar users interested in low domestic prices, are pressuring USDA to lower that percentage, while US sugar producers, interested in high domestic prices, are urging USDA to increase the percentage to at least 16.5. USDA also raised its estimate of 1997/98 domestic deliveries to 9.90 million short tons, up from the July estimate of 9.75 million tons. The higher demand figure offset some of the increased production forecast by USDA.

UNITED STATES - Sugar imports in May 1997 amounted to 280,672 tonnes, raw value, up from 180,093 tonnes in May 1996. This brought cumulative imports in the first eight months of 1996/97 (October/May) up to 1.768 million tonnes against 1.273 million tonnes in 1995/96. Total imports in 1995/96 reached 2.615 million tonnes against 1.557 million tonnes in 1994/95. Major countries of origin in 1996/97 were the Philippines with 230,555 tonnes raws against nil, the Dominican Republic with 228,347 tonnes, up from 110,653 tonnes and Guatemala with 214,882 tonnes compared to 198,583 tonnes. The largest suppliers of white sugar were Canada (20,553 vs 31,525 tonnes) and Mexico (20,496 vs 705 tonnes).

Sugar exports in May 1997 amounted to 8,724 tonnes, down from 31,481 tonnes in May 1996. This brought cumulative exports in October/May 1996/97 up to 107,172 tonnes compared to 225,145 tonnes in 1995/96. Total exports in 1995/96 were 310,341 tonnes compared to 504,854 tonnes in 1994/95. Major countries of destination in 1996/97 were Jamaica with 22,456 tonnes against 26,520 tonnes and Mexico with 16,865 tonnes compared to 24,591 tonnes.

DENMARK - The first Danish beet test of August 11 shows a high root yield whereas sugar content is below average. Root yield reached 37.10 tonnes per ha, sharply up on last year's 26.40 tonnes and also above the 30.36 tonnes of the five-year average (1992/96). Sugar content on the other hand was slightly down at 15.60 per cent against 15.70 per cent in 1996 and the average of 15.86 per cent. This resulted in a theoretical sugar weight of 5.79 tonnes of white sugar per ha, almost 40 per cent up on last year's 4.14 tonnes and 22 per cent above average. Hence, Denmark is heading for an excellent crop in 1997.

UNITED KINGDOM - The latest British beet test taken on August 11 shows that the crop is in excellent shape. Sugar content reached 15.77 per cent compared to 15.11 per cent in 1996 and also way above the five-year average (1992/96) of 15.40 per cent. Root weight amounted to 495 grams, up on 379 grams in 1996 and the average 416 grams. This resulted in a sugar weight per root of 78,06 grams, more than 36 per cent up on last year and 22.3 per cent up on the five-year average. Given an unchanged area sown to beet the data indicate an exceptionally good crop and barring unforseen changes last year's record result could be surpassed.

SWEDEN - The first Swedish sugar beet test of August 11 shows a rather high beet yield per ha while sugar content is lower than in 1996. Beet yield reached 29.00 tonnes against 22.10 tonnes in 1996, and the average of 27.52 tonnes (1992/96). Sugar content was 15.50 per cent against 15.80 per cent in 1996 and the average of 16.02 per cent. This resulted in a sugar weight of 4.50 tonnes, 29 per cent up on the 1996 result (3.40 tonnes) and 3 per cent above the average of 4.37 tonnes. Given an almost unchanged area sown to beet the Swedish sugar production in 1997 is likely to be up on the previous year.
F.O. LICHT - Our first estimate of the European beet sugar production 1997/98 will be released on Thursday, August 14, at 14.00 hrs central European time.
